launches.title: Bonbon - like LLMs learned math, our model independently learned the hidden rules of biology (NeurIPS 2026 Oral)
launches.tagline: Like LLMs learned math, Bonbon learned the hidden rules of biology
launches.body:
![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=129583&key=user_uploads/450746/d19e5852-af28-48f1-a9f4-894e36bf5e49)

**TL;DR: We built Bonbon, a vertical foundation model for biology. Bonbon developed emergent biological capabilities and independently learned the hidden relationships governing molecular interactions, just as LLMs learned math without being explicitly trained on it. Bonbon opens a path to understanding biology as a complex system.** 

Bonbon was accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 main track as an **Oral, top 0.4% of submissions**, and is, to our knowledge, the first model to exhibit emergent biological reasoning about molecular interactions. 

Bonbon also works well in the lab on diverse disease targets, including ones it never saw before, and discovers structurally novel molecules different from anything known in the literature to work on those targets.

We spent two years on this quietly, taking a first principles approach and building a new architecture and a proprietary dataset of about 3.2 trillion tokens. We are now excited to share what happened when we put these together and scaled our model.

## Why we built it

AI models have learned to write, reason, and code, yet AI hasn't led to a major breakthrough in how we understand biology as a system. Models today are helpful in making a few isolated parts of drug discovery faster. They aim to solve one narrow problem at a time, like looking for binders that geometrically fit a protein target. But a molecule can fit a protein and still do nothing, or do the opposite of what you need. **The existing models are not helpful in better understanding biology as a system or expanding what drugs are possible to design.**

Biology is a complex system. How a cell behaves comes from millions of relationships working together, most of them still unknown to us. To make better drugs, we need to understand the system they act on. Today we mostly don't, which is why drug discovery is slow, expensive trial and error and so many diseases still lack good treatments.

So we built a model that independently learned these hidden relationships, to understand biology in its full complexity. **That's how we expand what's possible, not just accelerate what we already know.**

Our hypothesis was that the relationships governing molecular biology are encoded in the sequences of interacting molecules, and that with the right architecture, data, and training, they could be revealed. As we scaled Bonbon, we saw capabilities emerging across the hierarchy of biology. Bonbon learned on its own to answer biological questions that until now required lab experiments.

## What Bonbon learned

We trained Bonbon on sequences alone, with no structure coordinates, physics-based analysis, task-specific labels, or supervision. As we scaled it from 42M to 1.6B parameters, new capabilities appeared sharply at the largest scale. Here are some of the things Bonbon’s representation space reveals about a molecular interaction:

* **What it does:** Bonbon zero-shot predicts mechanism of action across six classes, including telling apart, on the same protein target, which molecules switch it on from those that switch it off. Today, this can only be measured through functional lab assays.
* **Where it happens:** Bonbon zero-shot localizes the binding site, including telling apart, on the same protein target, whether the interaction happens at the main site or a secondary one (orthosteric vs. allosteric). No existing computational method classifies orthosteric vs. allosteric engagement.
* **How it bonds:** Bonbon zero-shot recognizes covalent binding and pinpoints the specific residue that drives it. Existing covalent docking tools assume covalency up front. Bonbon infers whether covalency exists at all. 
* **Which atoms matter:** Bonbon zero-shot identifies the active part of the molecule, down to the atom level. Today, this is inferred through many long and expensive rounds of making and testing molecular analogs.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=129583&key=user_uploads/450746/3bf5fc96-a562-4ae1-b72a-75772c908e9e)

Each of these capabilities is important for drug discovery on its own. All capabilities were tested on proteins and molecules the model has never seen, showing Bonbon generalizes rather than memorizes.

Bonbon’s representation space collapses what is currently a chain of separate screens and assays into one inference pass. **This allows us to make the most ambitious medicines possible to design, and to put the hardest drug programs within reach.**

## Accurate, and 50,000× faster

The same representation space that gives rise to the emergent capabilities achieves state-of-the-art performance on widely used binding and affinity benchmarks. Bonbon's inference runs at 2,500 molecular interactions per second on a single H100, about 50,000× faster than leading co-folding models, without compromising accuracy. It's built for the scale of biology, where the questions span millions or billions of interactions.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=129583&key=user_uploads/450746/8f3c5b43-ebac-44ac-8eac-67d93b1def9f)

## Bonbon works in the lab and discovers new chemistry

We generated de novo molecules, Bonbon ranked them, and we tested across nine diverse disease targets of increasing difficulty. **Bonbon achieved a 61.5% dose-response hit rate** in assays performed by a CRO, compared to the \~0.1% typical of traditional high-throughput screening. Every tested molecule was less than 60% similar to anything in the training data, and Bonbon discovered **structurally novel molecules** not previously reported for these targets. 

Some examples:

* **HDAC6** is a target implicated in neurodegeneration. Most known HDAC6 inhibitors rely on hydroxamate chemistry, which has caused toxicity. Bonbon discovered novel non-hydroxamate inhibitors with chemistry not previously reported for HDAC6.
* **MNK2** is a cancer-related target with a narrow known chemical space. Bonbon discovered novel inhibitors outside the documented MNK2 chemistry.
* **VEGFR2 and ELANE** were both absent from Bonbon’s training data. Bonbon still discovered confirmed inhibitors for both, showing that Bonbon transfers to targets it had never learned from.

![uploaded image](/media/?type=post&id=129583&key=user_uploads/450746/1c26d9d7-32b6-4dcd-b4f9-cbd191cb59cd)

## What's next

Bonbon reasons across many relationships of every interaction, at the scale of biology. This is the foundation for moving from individual molecular interactions to pathways, living cells, and eventually understanding and controlling entire biological systems. We are already extending Bonbon toward entire cells. More soon.

## Who we are

* [@Adi Mashiach](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/450746)**:** physician, machine learning researcher in systems biology, and third-time founder. Founded Nyxoah (NASDAQ: NYXH) and Innovea (acquired). 85+ US patents. Invented and built Mechanistic Reasoning, the architecture behind Bonbon.
* [@Mirella Mashiach](https://bookface.ycombinator.com/user/741327)**:** pharma executive and investor who understands the limitations of current drug discovery. Former Managing Director of Teva’s $200M corporate venture fund and VP of BD and Strategy at Teva Pharmaceuticals.

**Collaborate:** [Push biology further with Bonbon](https://www.outputlabs.ai/collaborate).

**We're hiring** in NYC/SF:[ MTS, Pretraining](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/output-labs/jobs/bcIFoMY-member-of-the-technical-staff-pretraining),[ MTS, Molecular Generation](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/output-labs/jobs/xNEItqX-member-of-the-technical-staff-molecular-generation),[ MTS, Biological Data](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/output-labs/jobs/MGz9Bnv-member-of-the-technical-staff-biological-data),[ MTS, Interpretability](https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/output-labs/jobs/4yKMT2W-member-of-the-technical-staff-interpretability).
